title: American Mass Media
description: (COMM 1307) American Mass Media. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the development and role of mass media in the United States across print, broadcast and digital platforms. Surveys ways journalism, entertainment, advertising and/or social media industries have evolved alongside major legal, economic and technological changes. Examines how media shape public understanding of news, culture and community life. Course content may reference current events or contested media topics for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds media literacy essential for participation in contemporary information environments. Supports workforce preparation for fields involving communication, marketing, journalism, public relations, policy and content creation. Strengthens ability to interpret media systems and evaluate messages. Provides academic grounding for further study in media, communication and related social sciences, while promoting informed engagement with public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers ways media messages are not neutral transmissions of facts or entertainment, but are reflections of institutional structures, economic incentives and cultural values. Clarifies differences between news, opinion, analysis, persuasion and/or misinformation, enabling critical comparison. Considers responsible media as involving critical interpretation, evidence assessment and awareness of perspective. Applies media literacy concepts to support informed citizenry through an understanding of First Amendment protections. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of media history and industry development; journalism and press freedom; advertising and entertainment business models; media law and ethics; corporate ownership and consolidation; social media platforms and audience participation; representation in film, television and news; and the role of media in elections, crisis coverage or cultural debate. Course materials may include real-world examples that involve political and/or social controversy, examined for purposes of understanding the role of media in the United States and around the globe.

title: Mass Media Information
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores methods for locating, verifying and organizing information for use in journalism and related media fields. Examines how reporters, researchers and content creators identify credible sources, interpret data and manage competing forms of evidence. Covers procedures for working with public records, interviews, documents and digital databases. Introduces basic interview techniques and requires a range of interviews. Addresses legal and ethical standards guiding information access, attribution and responsible use. May reference real-world news events and/or disputed claims for purposes of evaluating information practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies directly to careers in journalism, public communication, strategic media, research and content production where accuracy and credibility are essential. Builds fluency in information gathering and source evaluation for professional settings such as newsrooms, nonprofit advocacy, policy communication and organizational messaging. Supports academic preparation for advanced coursework in reporting, media law, research methods or data journalism. Strengthens civic readiness by reinforcing principles of evidence-based decision-making in public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how information is not merely “found” but actively selected, framed and interpreted through methodological choices. Highlights differences between rumor, opinion and verifiable fact, while showing how even credible sources may present information with limitations or bias. Considers that responsible information gathering requires transparency in process as much as accuracy in outcome. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include source credibility and verification; interviewing and data collection methods; public records and open-source intelligence; fact-checking and revision protocols; digital search strategies; statistical interpretation and data visualization; legal frameworks governing access and privacy including public records legislation at the federal and state levels; ethical considerations in handling sensitive or incomplete information. May draw on journalism, government documents, nonprofit reports or corporate communications when relevant to understanding differences in information intent and reliability.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 ; freshman or sophomore classification; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.

title: Media Writing I
description: (COMM 2311) Media Writing I. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores foundational practices of news and media writing across print, digital and broadcast formats. Covers core principles of reporting, source development, interviewing, story structure, clarity, accuracy and ethics. Emphasizes deadline writing and editorial standards such as Associated Press style. Includes both classroom instruction and lab-based field reporting and/or writing practice. Course content may reference current events or public controversies as real-time reporting contexts, examined for purposes of journalistic analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds competencies essential for careers in journalism, public communication, media production and content strategy, including information gathering, source evaluation, editing and professional writing. Supports preparation for advanced coursework in reporting, multimedia storytelling, strategic communication or public affairs. Provides transferable skills for civic participation by strengthening the ability to assess evidence, verify claims and communicate clearly in public-facing formats. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights the difference between everyday writing and journalistic writing defined by professional standards of fairness, attribution, style and verification. Considers that responsible reporting involves interpretation, fact assessment, and acknowledgment of perspective without slant or speculation. Develops recognition of how word choice, structure and sourcing shape public understanding. Analyzes how news stories serve both individuals and communities. Develops understanding of professional ethics standards. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of news values, interviewing techniques, attribution and quoting, hard news and feature formats, multimedia writing, legal constraints and ethical dilemmas in reporting. Exercises may involve real or hypothetical scenarios involving crime, politics, social issues or public institutions, used solely to develop reporting judgment and writing skills.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 102 and JOUR 200 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.

title: Television Sports Production
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how televised sports are produced behind the scenes, from planning to live execution. Introduces the roles of producers, directors, announcers, camera operators and technical crews, emphasizing collaboration across production teams. Examines historic developments in sports broadcasting alongside contemporary industry practices, including graphics, replay operations and/or real-time storytelling. Course content may reference high-pressure or emotionally charged broadcast situations for the purpose of professional analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops workforce-ready skills in research, coordination and deadline-driven collaboration through engagement with live event production and sports media workflows. Provides practical experience in broadcast storytelling, technical setup and real-time decision-making. Builds foundations for effective communication under pressure, rapid problem-solving and teamwork, competencies that transfer to careers in media, athletics, production management and other professional or academic settings requiring precision and adaptability. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how sports broadcasting functions as both entertainment and institutional messaging, shaping narratives of competition, identity and community. Examines ways production choices, such as camera angles, commentary, graphics and pacing, frame audience perception. Informs reflection on how spectacle, emotion and/or technology intersect in mediated sport. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of broadcast history and industry structure; producer and director decision-making; live graphics and replay systems; commentary and on-air performance roles; camera work and technical operations; crisis management during live events; ethics of representation in sports storytelling; evolution of streaming, social media integration and fan engagement. Course materials may include footage depicting intense competition, injury or heightened emotion, examined for purposes of professional critique.

title: Interviewing - Principles and Practice
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of interviewing as a purposeful form of interpersonal communication. Focus on questioning strategies, listening and interaction between the interviewer and interviewee. Examines informative, persuasive, survey and/or employment interview contexts. Develops skills as both the interviewer and the interviewee. Emphasizes how structure, audience, goals and setting shape communication choices. Addresses the logical and psychological bases of interviewing. Class applications may involve exposure to perspectives and experiences across social, cultural and professional backgrounds. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds transferable skills essential to journalism, media, public communication and organizational practice. Involves questioning, listening, adaptation to audience and purpose and interaction across varied goals. Applies to situations that require navigating unfamiliar or sensitive territory with professionalism. Develops skill in effectively navigating differences in belief, identity, experience and disagreement within interview contexts. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how interviews function as purposeful conversations, showing how credibility, preparation and strategy shape outcomes. Encourages awareness of the interview as a structured exchange rather than spontaneous talk. Broadens understanding of how perspective and authority influence communication across roles and settings for both interviewer and interviewee. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of questioning techniques, listening practices, rapport-building, credibility assessment and ethical responsibility; examination of informative, persuasive, survey, research and/or employment interviews; consideration of how audience, purpose and context govern interview structure and performance. Course work may involve engagement with people from varied backgrounds and experiences. Interview practice may include topics connected to identity, culture, ethics, work and/or participants’ personal lives. Exposure to differing viewpoints and/or lived realities reflects the range of issues encountered in professional and public communication. May include resume writing skills in preparation for career interviews.
prerequisites: Cross Listing: COMM 215/JOUR 215 .

title: Communication Technology Skills
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines principles and practices of communication technology in the digital domain. Surveys the history and standards of television, radio, video gaming, streaming media, e-publishing and/or social networking industries and markets. Focuses on production skills such as composing, recording and editing digital content, as well as media literacy across platforms, including the ability to evaluate social, cultural and/or ethical implications of communication technologies. Emphasizes media-centric strategic foresight to postulate regarding the future of the communication and technological landscape. Class applications may also draw on popular culture and/or current events, connecting course concepts to contemporary media environments. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds technical competence and media literacy skills applicable across professional, academic and civic contexts. Develops the skills necessary to create digital media content, adapt communication strategies to emerging technologies, tell stories across multiple media platforms and evaluate the impact of communication technologies on audiences and industries. Strengthens preparation for careers in journalism, media production, marketing, communication design, public relations and related fields where technological fluency and critical analysis are essential. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Builds understanding of how communication technologies shape interaction, identity and/or culture beyond their technical functions. Highlights how tools such as streaming platforms, social media and/or virtual environments influence professional practice, everyday communication and public dialogue. Clarifies both opportunities and challenges presented by digital media, including questions of access, ethics and/or social impact. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of the development and application of communication technologies across industries; exploration of audio, video, web and interactive media tools; analysis of digital platforms and markets; consideration of issues such as media convergence, intellectual property, ethics and sociocultural impact. Course work may incorporate case studies from popular culture and/or current events to connect course concepts with real-world practices. The course may include discourses and perspectives that are unfamiliar or controversial, reflecting the diversity of discourses relating to digital technologies and practices.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Enrollment in communication or telecommunication media studies majors, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor. Cross Listing: COMM 230/JOUR 230 .

title: Podcasting and Audio Storytelling
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores basic audio storytelling techniques required for podcast production within journalism and digital content creation, including principles of podcast development, scripting, interviewing, voice performance, audio recording and editing. May include instructions in microphone selection, sound environments and use of editing software. Covers branding elements such as titles, descriptions, cover art, music and metadata. Introduces strategies for publishing, promotion and audience growth across distribution platforms. Course content may include legal and ethical considerations related to privacy, attribution, licensing or defamation. Course content may reference real-world events or personal narratives for purposes of analysis and production rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops production skills applicable to careers in journalism, strategic communication and digital content creation. Promotes skills in narrative design, research organization, technical proficiency and navigating teamwork in creative industry contexts. Supports academic preparation in media writing, audio reporting and multimedia storytelling. Enhances civic communication skills by training attention to voice, perspective and accountability in public messaging. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights differences between casual conversation and structured audio storytelling designed for listeners’ attention. Clarifies how tone, pacing, editing and sound design influence interpretation and credibility. Encourages recognition of ethical responsibility when representing others’ voices or lived experiences in recorded form. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of podcast formats and genres; interview preparation and questioning techniques; narrative scripting; ambient sound and music beds; recording equipment and vocal delivery; editing workflows and mixing practices; platform distribution and analytics; audience design and engagement. Course material may draw on real-world audio examples involving sensitive or emotional content, used for purposes of critical listening and professional development.
prerequisites: Cross Listing: COMM 248/JOUR 248 .

title: New Media and the Independent Voice
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of new and independent media in shaping cultural, political and social life. Surveys forms such as blogs, podcasts, video, digital storytelling and social media platforms. Considers how independent voices create, challenge and reshape narratives in communities and public discourse. Attention to the relationship between personal voice, creativity and professional practice, as well as to issues of credibility, trust, ethics and representation. Explores how traditional and independent media engage with topics including activism, identity, politics and/or popular culture, highlighting both opportunities and challenges for communication in digital environments as they are constantly evolving. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds media literacy and production skills relevant to journalism, communication, marketing and/or creative industries. Develops competence in analyzing the credibility, reach and influence of independent media. Strengthens preparation for roles requiring digital fluency, critical thinking and the ability to adapt messages across platforms. Provides tools for both professional communication and civic engagement in a media environment shaped by independent voices. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how independent media can be both a space of empowerment and a site of contestation. Highlights how digital platforms amplify personal, cultural and political voices, while also raising ethical and practical challenges. Highlights how identity, power and representation shape media production and reception. Develops understanding of the opportunities and limits of independent communication in contemporary society. Explores the opportunities and challenges presented by changes in the media landscape. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of blogs, podcasts, video and social media platforms; exploration of digital storytelling and creative expression; consideration of ethics, representation and credibility in independent media; analysis of activism, politics and identity as expressed through digital platforms; evaluation of how independent voices influence communities, industries and public life. Course applications may draw on popular culture, current events and emerging issues. Discussions may also engage with controversial or contested topics, reflecting the role of independent media in addressing subjects that shape public dialogue.
prerequisites: Cross Listing: COMM 250/JOUR 250 .

title: Media Literacy in the Digital Age
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores mass media as a form of communication across cultural, political and creative contexts. Examines how news media, podcasts, social media, video, television and advertising are used to inform, persuade, critique and/or tell stories. Analyzes source, audience, message design and the relationship between medium and purpose. Examines how information, misinformation and disinformation spreads, developing skills and techniques for assessing credibility and verifying sources. Includes engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may arise through topics connected to politics, culture, ethics and/or lived experience. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices relevant to careers in media industries, strategic communication, journalism, political communication, public outreach, community outreach and digital content production. Involves skills relevant to designing messages, engaging audiences and producing or analyzing digital media across professional platforms. Prepares for advanced academic study in communication, media studies, journalism and related fields where digital fluency and critical media analysis are expected. Promotes awareness of how traditional media and independent media practices can contribute to civic discourse, cultural participation and emerging communication markets. Encourages media literacy in both communication careers and everyday life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how new media platforms differ from legacy communication systems in structure, purpose and power. Highlights the role of individual voice, audience interaction and platform design in shaping meaning and influence. Encourages recognition that public communication through digital media may challenge assumptions about authority, expertise and representation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis or creation of blogs, podcasts, social media campaigns, digital storytelling or multimedia commentary; exploration of how mass media engage politics, identity, culture and public issues; study of persuasion, narrative, audience engagement and message strategy in digital contexts. Assignments may involve analysis, production or both, depending on the instructor’s approach. Course materials may involve perspectives or content reflecting varied experiences, beliefs and interpretations encountered in contemporary media environments.
prerequisites: Cross Listing: COMM 255/JOUR 255 .

title: Introduction to Social Media
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores social media as a communication environment shaped by technology, audience, participation and platform design. Surveys major platforms, concepts and theories used to understand how individuals, organizations and communities create, share and interpret digital content. Examines how social media intersects with journalism, marketing, activism, entertainment and/or everyday communication. Considers how digital communication practices reflect and influence public discourse, society and culture. Engagement with real-world examples may involve topics connected to politics, religion, identity, ethics and/or lived experiences. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices connected to media industries, strategic messaging, journalism, advertising, nonprofit work, politics and other forms of public communication. Involves skills relevant to content creation, audience analysis, audience engagement, platform analysis and communication strategy. Connects to professional and academic paths in media, communication, journalism, marketing, public affairs and digital culture. Supports academic preparation to analyze ways social media shapes institutional messaging, cultural participation, community formation and civic dialogue. Develops applied skill in using social media strategically within entrepreneurial, organizational or community campaign contexts. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication via social media platforms differs from legacy media in participation, access and influence. Explores communication theories and strategies underpinning social media communication. Highlights tensions involving credibility, persuasion, privacy, visibility and/or identity in digital environments. Builds understanding of how platforms shape perception, behavior and communication norms in ways that are not always immediately visible. Supports informed assessment of one’s own media usage patterns and communication practices as case material for analysis. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication theories, platform histories and digital ecosystems; analysis of messaging strategies and audience behavior; consideration of digital identity, participation and online communities; exploration of ethics, credibility, privacy, representation and influence in online environments; examination of how platforms shape visibility, participation and public discourse; study of consent, branding, advocacy, journalism and influencer practices; comparison of interactive and traditional media. Course materials may reflect varied perspectives and examples from professional, cross-cultural and/or global contexts.
prerequisites: Cross Listing: COMM 275/JOUR 275 .

title: Careers in Communication and Journalism
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores fields and pathways in journalism, media and communication-related professions. Considers how professional interests, strengths and personality align with opportunities in media, public communication, journalism, strategic communication, digital platforms and related industries. Addresses foundational practices in networking, resume-writing, application material preparation, informational interviewing and digital presence. Includes exposure to campus resources and career planning tools. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of workforce expectations and industry pathways across communication-related professions. Introduces practical strategies for pursuing careers in media, advocacy, corporate communication, public affairs or related sectors. Assists in translation of classroom knowledge in securing internships, applied experience and long-term professional development opportunities. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication careers vary in purpose, setting and expectation. Highlights differences between common assumptions about media or communication work and the range of roles that exist across industries. Builds awareness of how skills, identity, professionalism and context shape access to and participation in communication fields. Provides support to students transferring into CMJR, promoting academic success and facilitating engagement with campus resources and communities. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include identification of career interests and strengths; exploration of communication professions and industries; development of application materials; digital portfolios and networking strategies; informational interviewing; engagement with professional resources and advising. Course activities may reference academic planning, campus involvement, workplace preparation and/or communications-specific career development. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis.
prerequisites: Cross Listing: COMM 280/JOUR 280 .

title: Directed Studies
description: Research problems related to communication field; individual work, fitted to special needs of specific student as determined by their interests and aptitude.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; approval of the program director.

title: Special Topics in...
description: Selected topics in an identified area of journalism and mass communication. May be repeated for credit.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Enrollment in USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor.

title: Research
description: Research conducted under the direction of a chosen faculty member in Journalism Studies. May be taken for a maximum of 3 hours credit.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Freshman or sophomore classification and approval of instructor.
repeatability: May be taken for a maximum of 3 hours credit.

title: Communication Law and Policy
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the legal and ethical foundations of communication in journalism, media and public life. Considers First Amendment principles, constitutional protections and limits on free speech and free press. Surveys key areas of communication law, including libel, privacy, copyright, obscenity, advertising, broadcast regulation and/or digital communication. Considers ethical standards and professional responsibilities that shape communication practices across diverse contexts. Directs attention to the tensions between individual expression, institutional regulation and public accountability. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in understanding how legal frameworks and ethical codes guide communication decisions in professional, academic and/or civic life. Builds skills for identifying risks, evaluating responsibilities and applying standards to journalism, media and/or organizational settings. Provides preparation for careers requiring knowledge of communication law, professional ethics and public accountability. Strengthens civic awareness by highlighting the role of free expression in democracy and public debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday assumptions about “free speech” and “freedom of the press” differ from their legal and professional realities. Encourages awareness of the limits, protections and obligations that accompany communication rights. Expands understanding of how legal rules intersect with ethical reasoning, professional standards and social expectations. Promotes careful reflection on how controversies over speech, press and media practice reveal broader tensions in democratic societies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of First Amendment foundations and constitutional principles; libel, privacy and copyright; obscenity, advertising and broadcast regulation; law and policy for digital and social media; ethical theories and professional codes; accountability, fairness, diversity and harm in communication practice. Course discussion may involve contemporary cases and controversial issues, addressed for purposes of legal and ethical analysis within an environment of respectful dialogue.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor; COMM-307 also taught at Galveston campus. Cross Listing: COMM 307/JOUR 301 .

title: The Mass Media and Politics
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication practices construct, circulate and contest political ideas and authority. Examines both how media influence political attitudes, participation and policy outcomes, and how political identity and conflict are shaped symbolically through news, entertainment, digital platforms and public rhetoric. Approaches may draw from social scientific models of media effects or rhetorical and critical analysis of political discourse. Emphasizes case-based evaluation of messages, sources and strategies across institutional, journalistic and citizen communication. Course content may include material involving political disagreement, conflict or graphic representation, examined for purposes of analysis rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops literacy in how political messages are constructed, distributed and interpreted across media systems. Applies to careers in journalism, political communication, public affairs, advocacy, research, law and civic or governmental work. Supports informed participation in democratic life by strengthening abilities to evaluate claims, recognize framing and distinguish between reporting, persuasion and manipulation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how politics is communicated not only through speeches or news outlets, but also through satire, visuals, entertainment formats, algorithmic feeds and policy messaging. Demonstrates how political messaging often blends information, symbolism and emotion to shape interpretation. Highlights the ways messages are interpreted differently depending on audience history, identity and media environment. Clarifies how communication shapes what counts as “fact,” “controversy” or “consensus” in public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of political news coverage, campaign strategy, advertising, agenda-setting, framing, propaganda models, political entertainment, social media activism and theories of representation. Consideration of media regulation, government communication practices, the influence of media on policymaking and the production of ideology. Course material may draw on historical and contemporary cases from local, national or international contexts, including disputed elections and outcomes, political controversies and crises, disinformation and surveillance, and contested social movements.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: POLS 206 or approval of department head; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 302 and POLS 302 .

title: Media Writing II
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Builds on foundational practices of news and media writing by shifting from structured exercises to more independent, publication-oriented work. Deepens proficiency in interviewing, sourcing, verification and AP style while introducing longer-form formats such as features, profiles, explanatory reporting and/or issue-driven narratives. Applies legal and ethical frameworks through scenario-based decision-making rather than rule recall. Reinforces core reporting habits of verification, accuracy and clarity, while advancing professional editorial readiness. May draw on current events or public controversies, addressed through journalistic standards of accuracy, attribution and fairness. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Provides practical experience valued in newsrooms, digital media, public affairs, nonprofit communications and content development roles requiring rapid research and fact-based writing. Strengthens transferable skills in information gathering, synthesis and public accountability, useful in academic and civic contexts where claims and sources must be critically evaluated. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how journalistic authority is earned through transparency, corroboration and structural discipline rather than voice alone. Builds awareness of framing choices — what to include, exclude or emphasize — and how these decisions influence audience interpretation. Examines reporting not only as information transfer but as ongoing negotiation between accuracy, access, ethics and presentation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include advanced interviewing techniques; background research and source vetting; feature and profile writing; beat development; editorial rewriting and collaborative critique; application of media law to reporting dilemmas; corrections and accountability practices; integration of photographs, headlines or multimedia assets based on publication constraints. May involve field reporting on campus or community issues, conducted within ethical and professional guidelines.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 203 , enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director.

title: Editing for the Mass Media
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles and practices of editing across print, broadcast and digital media, focusing on journalistic style and structure. Covers sentence-level refinement, fact-checking, clarity and consistency review, correction of grammatical and structural errors and adaptation of content for varied platforms and audiences. Emphasizes editorial judgment in tightening text without distorting voice or meaning. Includes headline and subhead writing, style guide application, peer-editing and awareness of how legal and ethical standards apply to editing decisions rather than reporting alone. Builds on media writing coursework by shifting focus from content creation to evaluation, revision and publication-readiness. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds advanced competencies central to newsroom, publishing, marketing and content strategy roles, including copyediting, information verification, editorial collaboration and style precision. Reinforces habits essential to academic and professional writing in fields where clarity, accuracy and/or credibility are required. Supports civic literacy by strengthening the ability to assess how wording, structure and omission influence public interpretation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how editing is not merely correction but interpretation, requiring awareness of audience, tone and implication. Considers how editorial choices shape storytelling, accessibility and fairness as much as writing choices do. Builds recognition of how cultural context, legal obligation and ethical norms factor into seemingly small changes. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include editing for grammar, structure and flow; fact-checking and error detection; AP style and style guide adaptation; headline and SEO writing; tone and audience calibration; legal and ethical considerations in revision; collaborative workflows between writers and editors; and analysis of published examples from news, nonprofit and commercial media. Exercises may draw from real or simulated stories involving sensitive or controversial subject matter, introduced for building skills at accurate and responsible editing practice.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 203 ; enrollment in JOUR major, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of program director; junior or senior classification.

title: Communication and Data Visualization
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores data as a form of communication and examines how information is interpreted, visualized and presented for different audiences and purposes. Emphasizes data storytelling as both an analytical and narrative practice, focusing on how visual choices shape understanding. Considers visualization designs that use data to inform, explain, persuade and/or support decision-making, using tools such as Excel and R. Addresses principles of visual perception, evidence-based messaging and interpretation of qualitative data and quantitative analyses, including descriptive and inferential statistics. Considers how visual choices, context and audience shape meaning in visual communication. Coursework may involve analysis, critique and/or development of data-driven messages in digital or visual formats. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds data visualization skills relevant to journalism, strategic messaging, marketing, public affairs, organizational communication, media production, research presentation and political advocacy. Builds capacity to interpret data, build visual explanations and representations and present insights in accessible formats. Supports effectiveness in academic and professional contexts where evidence, visualization and communication intersect. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how data gain meaning through interpretation, framing and visual design. Highlights the difference between raw information and communicative impact. Encourages attention to credibility, context and the persuasive or explanatory use of visualized evidence. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and critique of data visualizations; analysis of how charts, maps, dashboards, infographics or interactive visuals communicate meaning; consideration of audience adaptation, ethics, representation or narrative framing; exploration of digital storytelling strategies in data communication, including how sequencing, emphasis and interactivity guide interpretation; consideration of persuasive and informative uses of data in media, public communication, organizational settings or digital platforms. Course content may involve real-world issues or case studies that reflect diverse perspectives or public debate.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 303/JOUR 305 .

title: Digital Communication Analytics and Metrics
description: . COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of digital communication, data and the use of analytics to generate insight, evaluate communication strategies and inform decision-making. Examines techniques for extracting and interpreting information from websites, social media platforms and/or digital campaigns. Examines how data are used to assess audience behavior, platform performance, search engine optimization, message reach, engagement and/or return on investment. Considers how digital tactics connect across marketing, digital media platforms and communication research. Draws attention to the role of data in strategic planning. Course concepts are illustrated with examples that may involve digital communication in organizational, commercial, journalistic, political and/or nonprofit contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Promotes workforce preparation for careers in strategic communication, public relations, advertising, journalism, marketing, audience research and digital media. Advances understanding and skills related to interpreting performance metrics, applying measurement models and using analytics to support campaigns, outreach, reporting and/or organizational decision-making. Supports academic and professional work in areas where communication effectiveness, audience insight and data-informed planning intersect. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies the role of analytics in shaping communication strategy, storytelling and/or organizational decision-making. Highlights the difference between data collection and meaningful interpretation. Builds recognition of how digital communication practices intersect with privacy expectations, ethical obligations and the constraints of data tracking and measurement. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of web traffic, audience demographics and user behavior; study of paid, earned and owned media metrics; consideration of measurement models, platform dashboards and optimization tactics; exploration of data-driven decision-making, campaign evaluation, content performance, randomized field experiment and competitive research. Course examples may involve sectors such as journalism, marketing, nonprofit advocacy, strategic communication and/or politics, reflecting the varied uses of digital analytics in public communication.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Grade of B or better in COMM 275/JOUR 275 , COMM 323 , or JOUR 200 ; junior or senior classification. Cross Listing: COMM 304/JOUR 306 .

title: Photojournalism I
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores still photography practices in journalistic contexts, focusing on camera operation, composition, ethical standards and field-based image production. Emphasizes photography as a tool for documenting people, places, events and/or everyday life. Assignments simulate real-world photojournalism through location-based shoots, peer critique and portfolio development. Course content may involve exposure to newsworthy situations, including moments of conflict, hardship and/or public emotion, examined for the purpose of understanding practices of visual documentation and evaluating ethical and communicative impacts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competencies essential for careers in journalism, visual media, public relations, marketing and content creation, including technical literacy, deadline management, ethical decision-making and client/audience awareness. Supports preparation for advanced visual storytelling, multimedia reporting and professional communication roles requiring accuracy, clarity and visual credibility. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Builds understanding of how photographic choices such as framing, timing, proximity and editing can shape meaning as much as subject matter. Considers how journalistic imagery involves artistic judgment, public responsibility and industry codes of ethics. Builds awareness of how images circulate, persuade and/or inform differently across media platforms. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of news, feature, portrait, sports and event photography; composition, lighting and image sequencing; ethics of representation, consent and vulnerable subjects; history of visual journalism and iconic images; storytelling across single images and multi-photo narratives. Coursework may involve documenting diverse communities or public environments, approached with sensitivity to accuracy, fairness and professional standards.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

title: Social Media Law
description: Laws and regulations applied to social media, including communication law applied to enduring issues in the social media context; legal problems unique to social media; free speech, commercial speech and employment law as they affect individual users of social media as well as groups and organizations promoting points of view or products via social media, and employers.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 317/JOUR 317 .

title: Visual Journalism
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the analysis and creation of visual communication in journalistic and documentary contexts. Examines how photographs, illustrations, layout, color and digital design shape meaning across platforms such as news, magazines, social feeds and long-form multimedia projects. Traces aesthetic, technological and ethical developments in visual journalism while incorporating hands-on work in photography, design and digital illustration. Course content may involve exposure to controversial news imagery, including depictions of conflict, crisis and/or intense public emotion, for the purpose of developing visual judgment, ethical decision-making and critical analysis of journalistic documentation. Course content may also review editorial illustrations connected to opinion stories involving politics and/or cultural topics to develop an understanding of the impact of visual communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competencies needed in media professions where visual literacy, editing and/or content production are central. Supports preparation for careers in journalism, documentary work, publishing, advertising and digital communication by emphasizing visual judgment, technical execution and ethical decision-making. Strengthens academic pathways in media studies and provides transferable skills for civic participation in a visually driven information environment. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how images can inform, persuade and/or mislead depending on composition, context and display. Highlights the interpretive layers behind seemingly objective visuals, including choices of framing, editing, sequencing and captioning. Informs reflections on ways visual representation can intersect with questions of identity, credibility and public memory. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of photojournalism and reportage; layout and design principles; illustration and editorial graphics; data visualization and infographics; historical shifts in visual journalism; ethical and legal questions surrounding image use; and the influence of social media platforms on visual circulation. Creative components may involve curated image essays, design mockups or original photographic assignments completed within professional guidelines.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

title: Bilingual Reporting
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores journalistic reporting in Spanish and bilingual media environments. Covers foundational practices in newsgathering, interviewing, writing and/or audio storytelling conducted in both English and Spanish. Examines how bilingual journalists adapt style, tone and/or sourcing when communicating across cultural and linguistic audiences. Considers the distinct histories, media infrastructures and representational challenges associated with Latino/a and Spanish-language communities in the United States and around the globe. Coursework may include projects based on real-world local, national and/or international cases involving cultural identity, migration and/or public affairs. Spanish proficiency required. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds practical readiness for reporting roles in Spanish-language and bilingual media, as well as careers in public communication, community outreach, translation, podcasting and global media markets. Strengthens transferable communication skills valued in civic, nonprofit and governmental sectors that serve multilingual publics. Provides academic grounding for advanced study in journalism, Latino studies, global media or communication research. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how bilingual journalism involves more than translation; it requires cultural sensitivity, linguistic precision and ethical decision-making regarding representation and voice. Highlights differences in news values, sourcing practices and audience expectations between English-language and Spanish-language media. Informs reflection on how language choice can shift narrative emphasis, credibility and/or accessibility. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of bilingual interviewing; translation for journalistic accuracy; Spanish-language media history and market structures; ethics of reporting on immigration, identity, political conflict and cross-cultural communities; podcast scripting and audio editing; comparative analysis of Spanish and English newswriting conventions; trust-building and sourcing in marginalized or multilingual contexts; cross-national journalistic collaboration. Course content may include discussion of reporting on sensitive topics such as immigration, discrimination and political discord. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Instructors who teach this class may assign different readings and/or course topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; SPAN 302 or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: SPAN 319/JOUR 319 .

title: Mobile Journalism
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores multimedia reporting using mobile devices as primary tools for journalistic production. Covers techniques in audio gathering, digital still photography and video documentation, with emphasis on recording, editing, scripting and real-time publishing across multiple digital platforms. Simulates newsroom environments through deadline-based production, critique and revision. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds core competencies required in contemporary newsrooms and digital media industries, including rapid field reporting, technical versatility, editorial collaboration and/or content adaptation across platforms. Supports workforce preparation in journalism, strategic communication, digital content creation, nonprofit storytelling and public information roles. Reinforces transferable skills, including judgment under pressure, visual literacy and evidence-based storytelling, relevant to civic participation and public-facing professions. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights the distinction between casual mobile content creation and journalistic media production grounded in ethics, verification and clarity of purpose. Encourages critical reflection on how choices in framing, sequencing and platform affect audience interpretation. Demonstrates how professional credibility is constructed through transparency, accuracy and responsibility in visual storytelling. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of field recording techniques; audio scripting and narration; photo composition and ethical editing; video sequencing and interview setups; platform-specific publishing strategies; story pitching and editorial feedback; coverage of unfolding public events; ethical judgment and/or professional analysis. Assignments may involve documenting real-world environments — including emotionally charged settings or moments of conflict, controversy, hardship, celebration or vulnerability — approached for the purposes of visual analysis and responsible reporting.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

title: Media Industries
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the structures, economics and regulation of media industries across sectors such as film, television, music, publishing, video games, streaming and/or digital platforms. Examines how content is produced, financed, distributed and governed within commercial, public and hybrid systems. Considers trends in media ownership, labor practices, media convergence, globalization, audience markets and/or media policy. Attention to the roles of technology, culture and/or law in shaping how media industries operate. Course material may engage with real-world issues involving politics, regulation, representation and/or controversy, as relevant to understanding industry practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to careers in media production, media law and policy, journalism, strategic communication, entertainment management, marketing, publishing and digital platforms. Informs understanding of how media businesses make decisions, respond to regulatory pressures and adapt to changing technologies and audiences. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, business, law and policy. Useful for those navigating or analyzing industries shaped by ownership structures, market forces and cultural influence. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how media industries function beyond consumption and cultural familiarity. Highlights the interplay of economic interests, creative labor, technology and public policy. Encourages recognition of the power dynamics and institutional processes that shape media access, visibility and innovation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of media ownership and consolidation; production, distribution and exhibition systems; financing models and supply-chain relations; regulation and public policy; labor and creative work; technology and convergence; niche and mass markets; globalization and cultural circulation; media ethics and advocacy. Examples may draw on current and historical cases across major and emerging sectors.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 345 and FILM 345 .

title: Media, Culture and Identity
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how media and technology represent, reinforce and challenge ideas about identity, power and social differences. Examines theories of communication and culture to understand how media shape and are shaped by beliefs about race, gender, class, sexuality, ability, nationality and/or religion. Considers how communication practices construct and contest meanings of belonging, visibility and participation. Engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may involve topics that are culturally, politically and/or socially sensitive, discussed for the purpose of academic analysis and critical understanding. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Provides foundations for future professionals in journalism, digital media, strategic communication, public advocacy and related fields to anticipate audience response, avoid misrepresentation and build public trust. Builds transferable skills in media literacy, cultural analysis and ethical communication across professional and civic settings. Supports excellence in leadership and teamwork in diverse workplaces by considering how identity and difference influence communication dynamics. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, cultural studies and related areas concerned with diversity and representation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how cultural identities and media forms are interdependent, showing how meaning, power and visibility are negotiated through communication. Encourages reflection on the social roles of media institutions, creators and audiences in shaping public discourse and cultural imagination. Highlights the importance of dialogue, critical awareness and informed engagement in multicultural and mediated environments. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include representation and ideology in film, television, music and digital platforms; intersectionality and social identity; media and power; race, gender and sexuality in cultural production; class, globalization and inequality; disability and visibility; fandom, subcultures and participatory media; and contemporary debates around bias, equity and inclusion. Course material may include media content addressing real-world controversies or differing viewpoints, as relevant to understanding media, culture and identity.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 346/JOUR 346 .

title: Reporting Sports
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the principles and practices of sports reporting across professional, collegiate and community contexts. Covers live event reporting, interviewing, beat reporting, deadline writing and industry-standard formatting such as AP style. Emphasizes ethical judgment in reporting of competition, emotion and/or controversy, while maintaining neutrality, accuracy and professionalism. Simulates newsroom workflows through field reporting, editorial review and revision. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds applied competencies essential to careers in journalism, broadcasting, media relations, sports communication and content production. Reinforces transferable skills such as rapid information synthesis, audience adaptation, collaborative communication and deadline management. Supports broader workforce preparation in fields that require precise coordination, public-facing documentation and/or real-time decision-making. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how sports journalism blends entertainment, data, human interest and public accountability. Highlights the role of the journalist in navigating fandom, institutional access and representation, balancing narrative engagement with accuracy and fairness. Encourages awareness of how reporting choices influence perceptions of competition, identity and/or community. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include field interviewing; live coverage of sporting events; beat development; game recaps and feature storytelling; multimedia integration (audio, photo, mobile journalism); sports ethics and conflict-of-interest management; representation of athletes and teams across gender, race, class or institutional lines. Course material may involve observation or documentation of competitive, emotional and/or contentious sports environments, approached with sensitivity and professional responsibility.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

title: International Communication
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores key concepts, theories and practices in international communication and global journalism. Examines comparative media systems by analyzing how media develops across different political, cultural and economic contexts. Considers how world news circulates: who produces it, how it travels and how it is interpreted by diverse audiences. Examines issues such as freedom of the press, political propaganda, international advertising, public diplomacy and/or the impact of digital technologies. Students engage with theoretical, pragmatic, political and/or ethical perspectives to analyze how power, culture and/or technology shape global information exchange. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with tools for working with global media across cultural differences. Builds skills in evaluating international news, identifying propaganda and disinformation and applying ethical standards across cultures. Prepares students for careers in journalism, public affairs and related fields requiring cross-cultural awareness and media literacy. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Develops understandings of press freedom, news values and global information flows, recognizing that media systems operate within distinct political, cultural and economic contexts; exploring how interconnected stories affecting different countries and regions have developed through globalization and social media. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of comparative media systems; study of world news flows and international reporting; press freedom, censorship and ethics; political propaganda, public diplomacy and soft power; international advertising and global news cultures; impact of digital technologies, social media and generative AI; challenges of disinformation and “fake news” in global communication. Course materials may include discussion of sensitive or controversial topics, presented from multiple perspectives to reflect the diversity of global media.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; COMM-365 also taught at Qatar campus. Cross Listing: COMM 365/JOUR 365 .

title: Political Reporting
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Develops advanced reporting and writing skills through coverage of political actors, campaigns, institutions, policies and/or public debate. Emphasizes journalistic forms such as straight news, analysis, commentary, deadline reporting and/or long-form enterprise work. Coursework may involve interviewing public officials and stakeholders, sourcing public records, verifying factual claims and writing for publication under real-world time constraints. Engages legal and ethical challenges common to political reporting through case-based analysis and professional decision-making. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Prepares students for careers in journalism, strategic communication, public affairs, political campaign messaging and media production requiring accuracy, fairness and accountability in public-facing work. Reinforces transferable skills in source evaluation, poll evaluation, fact assessment, editorial judgment and deadline coordination. Supports media literacy and civic readiness by strengthening the ability to interpret competing claims and document political developments with clarity and restraint. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how journalistic credibility is constructed through sourcing, structure, transparency and consistency with professional standards. Highlights how political information circulates across formats such as news stories, speeches, commentary, newsletters, podcasts and/or social media. Encourages attention to how misinformation, framing or selective emphasis influence interpretation, requiring constant assessment of reliability and relevance. Explores ethical and legal issues regarding public records laws and the First Amendment. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and practice of interviewing, source development, fact-checking, news and feature structure, commentary and analysis writing, polling interpretation, deadline reporting and long-form enterprise work; consideration of media ethics, transparency, fairness and public accountability in coverage of elections, legislation, policy debates and/or political conflict. Course material may involve disputed events, competing narratives or controversial figures engaged for purposes of journalistic evaluation.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

title: Arts and Entertainment Journalism
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores reporting and writing practices specific to arts and entertainment journalism across genres such as film, music, visual arts, live performance, food and/or popular culture. Emphasizes feature writing, criticism and commentary, combining descriptive narrative with analytical evaluation. Includes regular drafting, revision and editorial feedback in workshop-style settings. Course material may reference real-world works or events that evoke strong personal and/or cultural responses; such content is approached through ethical journalistic standards of observation, fairness and critique. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops professional habits in research, interviewing, deadline writing and editorial collaboration relevant to journalism, reviewing, cultural reporting, media production, public relations and arts programming. Supports academic pathways in media criticism, narrative nonfiction and cultural studies. Reinforces transferable skills in analytical writing, public communication and civic engagement through responsible evaluation of cultural expression. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how arts and entertainment coverage blends storytelling with informed judgment, requiring both subject knowledge and ethical standards. Informs consideration of how tone, evidence and perspective shape credibility in evaluative writing. Explores how cultural journalism influences public conversation not by prescribing taste, but by modeling interpretation, context and reflection. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis and practice of feature profiles, reviews, cultural commentary and long-form narrative; genre-specific approaches to writing about art, food, music, theater, fashion, television and film; techniques for descriptive reporting and sensory detail; methods of comparative evaluation; ethics of criticism and representation. Course content may involve engagement with controversial works, sensitive subject matter or emotionally charged performances, addressed for purposes of journalistic analysis.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

title: Business Reporting
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the principles and practices of covering business, finance and the economy for general audiences. Emphasizes how companies, markets, government policy and consumer behavior intersect to shape everyday life. Trains students to locate, interpret and translate information from sources such as Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filings, economic datasets, industry reports and executive interviews. Coursework may draw on real-world developments involving corporate strategy, labor trends, inflation, energy, technology or regional economic change. Topics are approached through journalistic standards of accuracy, clarity and public accountability. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce preparation for careers in business journalism, data reporting, financial communications, public information and strategic media roles. Develops transferable skills in document interpretation, interviewing, trend analysis and deadline storytelling that apply across sectors including government, nonprofit, policy and corporate communication. Supports academic advancement in media studies, economics, public policy or analytics by reinforcing evidence-based reasoning and clear explanatory writing. Strengthens civic readiness by improving understanding of how economic decisions are communicated to the public and in turn affected by public response. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how business reporting is not limited to stock prices or balance sheets but involves explaining systems, including how decisions made by corporations, policymakers and markets influence employment, cost of living, infrastructure and opportunity. Informs consideration of the ways interpretation of economic data depends on framing, comparison and context. Considers ways clarity and fairness in economic reporting are essential to public trust. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of corporate filings and financial disclosure; market trends, labor shifts and cost-of-living metrics; economic indicators such as inflation, housing or consumer confidence; industry case studies across sectors such as energy, technology, retail or health care; regulatory and policy developments; and narrative approaches to profiling companies, entrepreneurs or local businesses. Course material may involve coverage of contested issues such as corporate incentives, taxation policy, wage debates and/or market volatility.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

title: Literary Nonfiction
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines long-form journalism and nonfiction storytelling grounded in factual reporting. Introduces literary techniques used in podcasting, personal essays, profiles, memoir-style narratives, investigative features and historical reconstructions. Emphasizes sourcing, documentation and ethical scene-building to distinguish literary nonfiction from fiction or opinion. May explore narrative formats across print, digital, audio and/or multimedia platforms. Content may reference real-world experiences involving hardship or sensitive subject matter, addressed through ethical journalistic standards. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops professional skills relevant to magazine writing, feature reporting, podcasting, documentary development and nonprofit or institutional storytelling. Reinforces competencies in interviewing, archival research, narrative framing, revision and editorial collaboration. Supports preparation for media careers, freelance writing and advanced study in communication or creative nonfiction. Strengthens ability to translate complex issues into compelling public narratives across civic, cultural and/or professional settings. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how narrative journalism balances storytelling craft with verification, transparency and fairness. Clarifies ethical boundaries around reconstruction, privacy and representation, including trauma-informed reporting practices. Encourages reflection on how perspective, access and documentation shape narrative authority. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include development of personal or reported essays; profiles and character studies; historical or archival-based narratives; place-based writing; investigative narrative structures; hybrid or experimental formats; collaboration with editors or fact-checkers; and discussion of contemporary debates around authenticity, voice and responsibility in nonfiction. May involve engagement with controversial issues, sensitive subject matter and/or emotionally charged topics, addressed for purposes of journalistic analysis.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

title: Global Media
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how globalization and media are intertwined across national, transnational and diasporic circuits. Explores frameworks for understanding globalization through media ownership, migration, representation, content flow, technology, everyday life and/or political influence. Considers how news, entertainment, advertising and/or digital platforms travel across regions and are reshaped by local and transnational values, communities and regulations. Highlights both integration and inequality in global media landscapes. Course content may reference political or cultural controversies, including propaganda, censorship, immigration or conflict reporting, for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of how media industries function in global markets, supporting preparation for careers in journalism, strategic communication, public affairs, media production, policy analysis and international business. Supports adaptability within multicultural and internationally connected workplaces. Develops abilities to assess media influence across national and cultural boundaries, relevant skills in organizations operating in global or multicultural environments. Strengthens academic grounding for advanced study in communication, media studies, international relations or cultural analysis. Supports civic literacy by clarifying how global media shape public opinion, diplomacy and perception between nations. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals that media are not neutral carriers of information but products of political, economic, ideological and cultural systems. Highlights how similar content can carry different meanings depending on context, history, ideology and/or regulation. Encourages reflection on how local and/or personal media environments are shaped by assumptions and practices that may differ substantially across national and cultural boundaries, fostering greater awareness of perspective and context. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of transnational media ownership and conglomerates; global circulation of news, entertainment and advertising; audiences and consumers; comparative media systems in democratic, authoritarian and transitional societies; localization and cultural adaptation; media policy, censorship and regulatory control; streaming platforms, social media and telecommunications infrastructure; migration, diaspora, citizenship and identity across borders. Course material may reference real-world cases involving political or cultural controversy, such as extremism, disinformation or state propaganda, for purposes of analysis and critique within an environment of respectful dialogue.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross Listing: COMM 458/JOUR 458 .

title: Sports Entertainment Reporting
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines journalistic storytelling within the evolving sports entertainment landscape. Explores formats ranging from narrative features and long-form commentary to rapid-cycle blogging, podcasts and fan-centered analysis. Emphasizes audience engagement, platform-specific voice and the blending of reporting, opinion and personality in sports media. Simulates newsroom or creator environments through recurring publishing deadlines and performance-based feedback. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds marketable skills for careers in sports journalism, content creation, digital media, public relations or brand communications. Reinforces professional practices such as sourcing, accuracy, editorial decision-making, audience strategy and ethical judgment under time pressure. Supports civic and cultural awareness by examining how sports intersect with identity, economics, politics and public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how sports coverage functions not only as entertainment but also as storytelling that frames community, rivalry, aspiration and controversy. Reveals distinctions between reportage, commentary, satire and hype, clarifying how credibility and influence can be negotiated across formats. Informs reflection on how fandom, access and commercial pressures shape journalistic tone and judgment. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis and production of sports blogs, feature stories, commentary pieces, social media threads, podcasts and/or multimedia packages. Consideration of athlete branding and influencer culture; fan communities and online discourse; ethics in sports reporting; representation and identity in sports narratives; commercialization of collegiate and professional athletics. May reference real-world cases involving controversy, misconduct and/or public debate when relevant to understanding communication choices in sports media.
prerequisites: Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

title: Magazine Feature Writing
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Develops advanced nonfiction storytelling skills through the study and production of magazine-length features, profiles, trend pieces, service journalism and/or first-person narratives. Emphasizes writing for publication across contemporary formats, including print, digital and/or multimedia environments. Involves pitching, researching, drafting and revising multiple feature-length articles under deadline, simulating professional editorial workflows. Includes analysis of publication style, voice and audience expectations across diverse magazine platforms. May involve coverage of current events or human-interest topics, approached through journalistic standards. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds professional competencies used by staff and independent writers within journalism, content strategy and media production, including interviewing, audience analysis, query development, revision and editorial collaboration. Supports preparation for publication-based careers as well as academic and civic contexts requiring long-form narrative communication, evidence-based reporting and/or clear voice. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how narrative journalism blends factual reporting with structure, scene-setting, characterization and perspective to build engagement while maintaining accuracy and accountability. Illuminates how credibility is earned through transparency, sourcing and stylistic discipline rather than formulaic structure. Encourages reflection on the responsibilities of representing real people and events in written form. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of profile writing, trend stories, service journalism, memoir and first-person features, pitch and query formats, magazine house style and voice, interviewing strategies, source documentation, revision techniques and editorial feedback processes. May involve field reporting, live story pitching and analysis of magazine departments or adopted publications. May draw on real-world reporting scenarios, ranging from lifestyle to public affairs, addressed with attention to fairness, accuracy and professional responsibility.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 203 ; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

title: Internship
description: Directed internship in a private firm or public agency to provide on-the-job experience appropriate to the student's degree program and career objectives. To be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Maximum of 3 credits may apply toward degree.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; enrollment in USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; approval of instructor; grade of C or better in JOUR 203 .

title: Directed Studies
description: Research problems related to communication field. Individual work, fitted to special needs of specific student as determined by his or her interests and aptitude.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; enrollment in USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; approval of instructor.

title: Special Topics in...
description: Selected topics in an identified area of journalism and mass communication. May be repeated for credit.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; enrollment in USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor; or approval of instructor.

title: Journalism as a Profession
description: COURSE OVERVIEW. Serves as an exit-level seminar for students completing advanced coursework in journalism. Synthesizes prior training in reporting, writing, editing, media law and ethics by requiring production of publication-quality work alongside critical reflection on journalism as a profession. Combines workshop-based writing development with discussion of contemporary issues facing news media, including questions of credibility, labor, technology and/or public trust. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens readiness for careers in journalism, media production, strategic communication and public information by refining writing portfolios, pitching skills, professional presentation and editorial collaboration. Provides preparation for workplaces that value initiative, ethical decision-making and long-form project management. Supports civic literacy by deepening understanding of journalism’s role in public accountability, information access and democratic culture. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights journalism not only as a set of skills but as an evolving institution shaped by economic pressures, technological change, audience behavior and ethical norms. Encourages recognition of the practical and moral challenges journalists face when balancing accuracy with speed, objectivity with transparency and access with independence. Reinforces that credibility emerges through verification, sourcing, clarity and sustained commitment to public responsibility. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include discussions of media credibility, fact-checking in high-risk environments, newsroom labor and diversity, long-form storytelling, press freedom, branding and career sustainability and journalistic responses to misinformation. May contain real-world reporting cases involving political conflict, legal disputes or sensitive human experiences, examined for purposes of professional analysis.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: JOUR 203 ; junior or senior classification; enrollment in JOUR major or JOUR minor; and approval of instructor.

title: Research
description: Research conducted under the direction of a chosen faculty member in Journalism Studies. May be taken for a maximum of 3 hours credit.
prerequisites: Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in JOUR 203 ; junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.
repeatability: May be taken for a maximum of 3 hours credit.
